title: Block close: character is daily
hook: the traits are built one day at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was open tent: see people early, go toward them, give more than you promise. Did you send the invitation? Today, the last day of this block on Mussar and Jewish ethics. Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

A jar of sourdough starter sits on a kitchen counter. Flour and water, a little bubbly, a little sour. Its keeper feeds it every day. Skip a day, and it sulks. Skip a week, and it may not come back. There is no feeding big enough to last a month. The starter lives on small, steady care, and in return it raises every loaf. Mussar treats character much the same way. This block began with one idea: work on a trait. Today, at the close, a look back at the traits, and at the daily feeding they need.
screen: `A JAR ON THE COUNTER.` → `FED EVERY DAY.` → `HOW CHARACTER STAYS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Turn it four ways. First, the map. This block walked through traits as measures, each with a right size: humility, patience, gratitude, order, calm, silence, truth, trust, zeal, generosity, honor, responsibility. Then speech: harmful speech, tales, slander, and speaking good. Then the hard ones, anger and envy, and Luzzatto's ladder up to holiness. Then ethics in the world: honest weights, not stealing minds, fair work, animals, waste, and the open tent. Second, repetition. Maimonides, in his laws of character, says that a person who wants to change a trait should practice the opposite act, again and again, until it comes easily and becomes part of who they are. Not a vow. A habit. Third, a thousand coins. The Mishnah, in Ethics of the Fathers, says the world is judged by the abundance of deeds. Maimonides, commenting on it, gives an example: someone who gives a thousand coins to one person at one time doesn't build the trait of generosity the way someone does who gives one coin a thousand times. The trait grows from the number of acts, not the size of one. Fourth, no finish line. Rabbi Tarfon says, in the same tractate, that it isn't yours to complete the work, and you aren't free to stop doing it. That is why Mussar, as this block met it, meant one trait at a time, an accounting of the soul at night, and beginning again the next morning. None of the traits in this block is learned in a day. Every one of them is learned daily.
screen: `TRAITS, SPEECH, LADDER, WORLD.` · `PRACTICE THE OPPOSITE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `ONE COIN A THOUSAND TIMES.` · `NOT YOURS TO COMPLETE, NOT FREE TO STOP.` · then, large: `CHARACTER IS DAILY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one trait for next month. Sit, and breathe. Let the traits from this block pass by: humility, patience, gratitude, truth, generosity, calm, speaking good, honest dealing, an open door. Notice which one tugs. Not the most impressive. The one your days actually need. Choose it. Then shrink it to one small act you could do every day: one thank-you, one honest sentence, one coin, one pause before answering. That act is the daily feeding. If you pray, you can ask for help with it in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Block close. Mussar and Jewish ethics: traits, speech, the ladder, and the world, built one act at a time. Today's word.

Your line: character is daily. Today, do your one small act for the first time, and write the trait somewhere you'll see it tomorrow. Next, a new block: the life cycle, from birth to death. Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In a Mussar group, a student may choose one trait to work on for a set stretch of time, practice a small daily act tied to it, and keep a short nightly journal of how the day went.

fork.setup: you want to become generous. you have a thousand coins to give. which way builds the trait, according to Maimonides?
options: give all thousand to one person at once.
give one coin at a time, a thousand times.
save them until you can give more.
fork.reveal: Maimonides says the trait grows from the number of acts, not the size of one gift: one coin a thousand times.

trapdoor: what you thought: good character is something you either have or don't.
what it means: a trait is built by small acts repeated daily, with no finish line.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides, Laws of Character, on practicing the opposite; his commentary on Avot 3:15, one coin a thousand times; Avot 2:16, Rabbi Tarfon.
